summary: Alex Volkov (W&B) and Benjamin Eckel (Dylibso/MCP.run) present on MCP observability at the AI Engineer World's Fair. The core problem: as agents adopt MCP tools, less code runs under developer control, creating an observability blind spot compounding with each tool added. W&B Weave announced MCP support via an environment variable for Python clients, but this only works when you control both client and server and is vendor-specific. To address broader needs, Volkov created observable.tools, a manifesto driving conversation toward vendor-neutral, standardized MCP observability. Eckel explains MCP-powered agents are distributed systems, making OpenTelemetry (OTel) the natural fit. OTel primitives covered: traces (tree of spans), spans (duration + metadata per step), syncs (centralized telemetry platforms), and distributed tracing (context propagation across services). Two scenarios exist: same-domain (you own both sides, can propagate context) and different-domain (third-party servers like GitHub/Stripe appear as black-box single spans). They achieved context propagation by passing OTel trace context through MCP's meta payload—an abuse of a lower-level interface needing higher-level tooling. Cross-language interoperability was demonstrated when a TypeScript agent sent traces to Weave (Python SDK) via OTLP with minimal code changes. Volkov shares a notable moment where Claude Opus 4, using Weave's own MCP server, discovered a support bot MCP tool and self-corrected its instrumentation by querying it—demonstrating agents autonomously fixing observability issues. Eckel announces MCP.run will export telemetry to OTel-compatible syncs for both its profiles (virtual composite servers) and task (scheduled/URL-triggered agent) features. They recap that observability exists in MCP today but is not evenly distributed. Calls to action: AI engineers should evaluate end-to-end observability; tool builders should create higher-level SDKs and work on semantic conventions (standardized span attributes so syncs understand what spans represent); platform builders should add OTel support and review RFCs. They reference the GenAI semantic conventions effort by the OTel team as a starting point.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the MCP Observability Problem
sections.summary: Alex Volkov (W&B) and Benjamin Eckel (Dylibso/MCP.run) introduce themselves and frame the problem: MCP adoption means less agent code runs under developer control, creating an observability blind spot that compounds as more tools are added. Both have been running MCP in production and found everyone solving observability in isolation.

sections.title: W&B Weave MCP Support Announcement
sections.summary: Volkov announces Weave MCP support via an environment variable (MCP trace list operation) on client and server, showing tool calls and durations. Demo shows client traces (red arrows) and tool calls like calculate BMI (blue arrows). Limitation: only works with Python-based clients and when you control both sides.

sections.title: Observable.tools Initiative and OpenTelemetry Primer
sections.summary: Volkov introduces observable.tools as a manifesto for vendor-neutral, standardized MCP observability. Eckel explains OTel primitives: traces (tree of spans), spans (duration + metadata per step), and syncs (centralized telemetry platforms/databases supporting a standard schema). OTel is becoming the global standard, adopted by Weave, Langfuse, and others.

sections.title: Distributed Tracing and Domain Scenarios
sections.summary: Eckel covers distributed tracing—stitching traces together when services send spans to the same sync. Two scenarios: different-domain (third-party servers like GitHub/Stripe appear as black-box single spans) and same-domain (you own both sides, can propagate context). Demo shows a Hacker News fetch agent as a black box, then with context propagation revealing an HTTP request (~350ms) and markdown processing.

sections.title: Context Propagation via MCP Meta Payload
sections.summary: Eckel explains how they propagate OTel trace context from client to server by shuttling data through MCP's meta payload—an undocumented lower-level interface. TypeScript example shows extracting current span and passing it to the server, which inherits it as parent span. Working demo available on GitHub. Eckel notes this abused the protocol and higher-level tooling should be provided.

sections.title: Cross-Language Demo: TypeScript Agent to Weave via OTLP
sections.summary: Because Weave supports OTLP, Eckel's TypeScript agent sent traces to Weave with minimal code changes—just defining Weave as the OTLP endpoint with authorization headers. Green traces show client side, server traces show internal calls. This demonstrates OTel's cross-language, cross-vendor interoperability for MCP observability.

sections.title: Meta MCP Story: Agent Self-Correction via Support Bot
sections.summary: Volkov shares a moment where Claude Opus 4, using Weave's own MCP server (which lets agents query and summarize trace data), discovered a support bot MCP tool on its own. The coding agent noticed traces showed up incorrectly, queried the support bot, received guidance, fixed the instrumentation, and verified the fix—all without human intervention. This demonstrated agents autonomously fixing their own observability issues.

sections.title: MCP.run OTel Export Announcement and Recap
sections.summary: Eckel announces MCP.run will export telemetry to OTel-compatible syncs, covering both its profiles feature (slicing/dicing multiple MCP servers into one virtual server) and its task feature (a single-prompt agent triggered via URL or schedule). Volkov recaps that observability exists in MCP today but is not evenly distributed, and the community needs to come together to create tooling and conventions.

sections.title: Call to Action and Semantic Conventions
sections.summary: Calls to action across three audiences: AI engineers should evaluate end-to-end observability of their MCP execution chains; tool builders should create higher-level SDKs and work on semantic conventions (standardized span attributes so syncs can distinguish e.g. an HTTP 200 from an MCP tool call error), referencing the GenAI semantic conventions effort by the OTel team; platform builders should add OTel support and review RFCs. Both speakers share final contact info: Eckel promotes MCP.run (free account), Volkov promotes W&B Weave MCPOP, observable.tools manifesto, and the ThursdAI podcast.
